issue.body:
Sponsors SeaweedFS via Patreon https://www.patreon.com/seaweedfs
Report issues here. Ask questions here https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/seaweedfs
Please ask questions in https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/discussions

**Describe the bug**
Let me show you the behaviour, the client I used was minio client. with seaweed version 3.53 and 3.43
```shell
# using weed version 3.53
$ mc ls weed-admin/images/reverse_bag_images/
# NO OUTPUT FOR THE ABOVE COMMAND
$ mc ls weed-admin/images/reverse_bag_images
[2023-07-12 12:06:09 +07]     0B reverse_bag_images/

[2023-07-12 12:13:19 +07]     0B 2023-07-03/
```

issue.body:
## Summary

Addresses https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/7299

This PR adds two new configuration options for Redis filer stores:

### 1. Username Support
Added `username` configuration to:
- `redis2` store
- `redis_cluster2` store  
- `redis_lua` store
- `redis_lua_cluster` store

(The sentinel stores already had username support)

### 2. Key Prefix Support
Added `keyPrefix` configuration to **all** Redis stores. The prefix is prepended to all Redis keys, which is useful for:
- Envoy Redis Proxy setups to redirect keys to specific Redis clusters
- Multi-tenant Redis deployments
- Key namespace isolation

### Example Configuration

```toml
[redis2]
enabled = true
address = "localhost:6379"
username = "my-seaweedfs-user"
password = "secret"
database = 0
keyPrefix = "seaweedfs:"
```

### Files Changed
- `weed/filer/redis2/*.go` - Added username and keyPrefix support
- `weed/filer/redis_lua/*.go` - Added username and keyPrefix support
- `weed/command/scaffold/filer.toml` - Updated configuration template

issue.title: filer: opt-in inode->path index with shell nfs.enable / nfs.disable
issue.body:
Groundwork for bringing back the `weed nfs` gateway. The gateway resolves NFS filehandles by reversing an inode to its path, which the deterministic hash inode cannot do, so the filer needs a reverse index — but nobody should pay for it unless they export something.

- filer.conf `PathConf` gains an `inode_index` option. The store wrapper writes inode->path rows only for entries under a marked location; with no rule (the default) no index work happens at all. Every filer picks the rule up through the normal filer.conf reload, so there is no per-process flag to keep in sync across a cluster.
- `nfs.enable -path=/exports -apply` marks the path and backfills rows for the entries already under it, assigning inodes to entries that predate filer-assigned inodes, so pre-existing files resolve by filehandle immediately. Re-running is idempotent.
- `nfs.disable -path=/exports -apply` removes the mark and deletes the rows, so turning NFS off leaves no index data behind.

Verified against a live server: enable backfills exactly the in-scope entries, files created afterwards get rows through the filer-side hook, out-of-scope paths get nothing, and disable clears every row.

The gateway restore itself comes as a follow-up on top of this.

issue.title: filer: honor the documented TLS options in every redis store
issue.body:
`filer.toml` has advertised `enable_tls`, `ca_cert_path`, `client_cert_path` and `client_key_path` under `[redis2]`, `[redis2_sentinel]` and `[redis_cluster2]` since mTLS was added, but only the plain `redis2` and `redis3` stores ever read those keys, and they read `enable_mtls` rather than the documented `enable_tls`. So a sentinel or cluster deployment that set the documented knobs connected in plaintext with no complaint - which is the case that needs TLS most, now that sentinel credentials travel on the wire.

The TLS config now lives in `weed/filer/redis_tls` and all six redis stores use it: `redis2`, `redis2_sentinel`, `redis_cluster2`, `redis3`, `redis3_sentinel`, `redis_cluster3`.

Behavior:

- Both `enable_tls` and `enable_mtls` turn TLS on, so existing configs keep working under either name.
- `ca_cert_path` is optional and falls back to the system roots, and the client key pair is optional too, so `enable_tls = true` alone works against a server that only does server auth.
- Cert and CA load failures return an error out of `Initialize` instead of calling `glog.Fatalf` from inside the store.
- `ServerName` is no longer pinned to the configured address. `tls.DialWithDialer` fills it in from whatever address go-redis dials, which is what the sentinel and cluster clients need since they talk to several hosts and discover the master at runtime. For the single-address stores the derived name is the same one that was being set by hand.

Covered by unit tests on the config builder: disabled, either enable key, missing/garbage CA file, and a client cert without its key.

issue.title: Redis connection pool issue with redis2_sentinel backend
issue.body:
Hello,

I am using SeaweedFS filer v4.17 with redis2_sentinel as metadata store. Recently, we observed Redis connection pool related errors in filer logs during Redis Sentinel master changes.

Environment:
- SeaweedFS: v4.17
- Filer store: redis2_sentinel
- Redis: 7.2.4
- Redis Sentinel: 3 nodes cluster

We have verified the following:
1. Redis Sentinel status is normal.
2. Redis master information reported by Sentinel is correct.
3. Filer configuration is using redis2_sentinel.
4. Redis client related configurations have been checked, including Sentinel configuration, and no abnormal configuration was found.

The observed scenario:
1. Redis master was running normally.
2. Redis Sentinel changed the master node (through failover).
3. The filer process continued running without restart.

After the master switch, filer occasionally reported:
`redis: connection pool: failed to get a usable connection after X attempts`

We would like to understand the expected behavior of the redis2_sentinel backend in this situation.
Questions:
1. When Redis Sentinel switches the master, how does SeaweedFS handle existing Redis connections in the connection pool?
2. Are Redis connections created before the master switch automatically detected as invalid and removed from the pool?
3. If old Redis connections remain in the pool temporarily after the master switch, can they cause errors such as "failed to get a usable connection"?
4. After Redis Sentinel master switch, should filer recover automatically without restart?

We would appreciate any suggestions on whether this behavior is expected or if there are additional configurations we should check.

comments.body:
Answers in order, then what I changed.

1. Nothing SeaweedFS-specific happens. The client is a go-redis failover client, which subscribes to the sentinels' `+switch-master` channel; when a switch arrives it walks the pool and closes every connection whose remote address is not the new master. New connections are dialed through the sentinels, so they land on the promoted node.

2. Only once that switch is observed. Connections already checked out, and any picked up in the window before the notice arrives, are not pre-emptively invalidated - they fail on use and are dropped then.

3. Yes. `redis: connection pool: failed to get a usable connection after N attempts` is a go-redis log line from the pool, not an error returned to the caller: the pool skipped the idle connections it had and dialed a fresh one instead. Seeing it clustered around a failover is expected. What actually hurts is the wait in front of it.

4. It should, without a restart, and the delay you saw was ours. The sentinel store hardcoded `ReadTimeout: 30s`. So every request that grabbed a connection to the dead master blocked a full 30 seconds before that connection was retired, and since go-redis derives `PoolTimeout` from the read timeout (read timeout + 1s), everyone else queued behind them for ~31s. The other redis stores use the go-redis default of 3s.

#10441 drops the hardcoded timeouts and makes the go-redis dial, timeout and pool settings configurable per store section - `read_timeout_millisecond`, `pool_size`, `pool_timeout_millisecond`, `conn_max_lifetime_seconds`, `max_retries` and so on. Unset keys keep the go-redis defaults, so `redis2_sentinel` now fails over on a 3s read timeout like every other redis store, and you can set `read_timeout_millisecond = 30000` to get the old value back if some of your commands are genuinely that slow.

Hi Chris,

Thanks for the detailed explanation and the fix.

Your explanation helps us understand the behavior. We confirmed that the issue was related to the Redis Sentinel failover scenario, where existing connections pointing to the demoted master may block until the read timeout expires, causing the connection pool to become temporarily unavailable.

We noticed that the fix is included in PR #10441, but it does not seem to be merged into the current master branch/released version yet.

Could you please advise:
1. Will this fix be included in the next SeaweedFS release?
2. Before the new release is available, is there any recommended workaround for SeaweedFS v4.17 users to reduce the impact of this issue?  For example, can we safely adjust the Redis timeout related settings manually, or is upgrading the preferred solution?

Thanks again for your help.

issue.title: filer: make the redis connection settings configurable
issue.body:
Fixes #10438

The sentinel stores hardcoded `ReadTimeout: 30s`, `WriteTimeout: 5s`, `MinRetryBackoff: 100ms` and `MaxRetryBackoff: 1m`. go-redis does retire the pooled connections to the demoted master on `+switch-master`, but anything already holding or picking one of those connections blocks for the full read timeout first, and `PoolTimeout` defaults to read timeout + 1s, so under load every other caller queues behind them for ~31s. That is what a filer looks like when it is "not recovering" from a sentinel failover, and there was no way to shorten it.

The other redis stores took the go-redis defaults with no knobs at all.

So: drop the hardcoded values and read the dial, timeout and pool settings from the store section, for every redis store (redis, redis2, redis3 and their cluster/sentinel variants). Each key keeps the go-redis default when unset, so the only behavior change is on the two sentinel stores, which now get the same 3s read timeout as everyone else and can be tuned back up with `read_timeout_millisecond = 30000` if a deployment needs it.

New keys, accepted by every redis store section:

```
max_retries                        # 0 is three retries, -1 disables retrying
min_retry_backoff_millisecond
max_retry_backoff_millisecond
dial_timeout_millisecond
read_timeout_millisecond
write_timeout_millisecond
pool_size
pool_timeout_millisecond
min_idle_conns
max_idle_conns
conn_max_idle_time_seconds
conn_max_lifetime_seconds
```

issue.title: Lazily-created remote-mount entries carry no TTL and accumulate without bound
issue.body:
All references are to `master` @ `db5a086d0` (4.41).

## Problem

Under a lazy remote mount, filer entries are created on demand: `maybeLazyFetchFromRemote` on a miss in `FindEntry` (`weed/filer/filer_lazy_remote.go:30-117`) and `maybeLazyListFromRemote` on a directory listing (`weed/filer/filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:32-173`). Both create remote-only mappings — a path pointing at an object in the remote store — and neither sets `TtlSec`, so it stays `0` and nothing ever expires them.

They therefore accumulate one entry per distinct object ever touched, and are never reclaimed. On one of our filers that is currently **11,142,152 entries, growing by roughly 330,000/day**, with no upper bound short of the object count of the bucket.

The mount's own cache TTL does not help: `ListingCacheTtlSeconds` only decides how often a directory is re-listed from the remote (`filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:60-76`), and re-listing an existing entry takes the merge path at `:107-120`, which updates it. Nothing removes anything.

This is a real operational ceiling for anyone fronting cloud storage with a shared filer store. The entries are trivially reconstructible — the remote is authoritative, and a filer that lacks an entry re-derives it on the next access via exactly the code that created it.

## Why plain TTL is the right mechanism

The filer already has expiry machinery that does precisely what a cache wants, and — importantly — the *plain* TTL path never touches the remote:

- `FindEntry`: `f.Store.DeleteOneEntry(ctx, entry)` then `ErrNotFound` (`weed/filer/filer.go:434-437`);
- `doListDirectoryEntries`: expired entries collected at `:473-476` and deleted via `f.Store.DeleteOneEntry` at `:496-500`.

Both go to the store and nothing else. Neither reaches `doDeleteEntryMetaAndData`, so `maybeDeleteFromRemote` — which is gated on `!isFromOtherCluster` inside it (`weed/filer/filer_delete_entry.go:144-152`) — is not on that code path at all. Expiring a cached entry **cannot** propagate a delete to the remote object.

Worth having on the record: the S3-lifecycle branch a few lines above behaves differently. It calls `f.doDeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, entry, true, false, nil)` (`filer.go:429` and `:492`) with `isFromOtherCluster: false`, so it *does* reach `maybeDeleteFromRemote` and *does* propagate. Whatever is decided here, those two expiry paths are not interchangeable for remote-mounted content.

No new job, no sweep, no schedule — the reclamation is already written.

## Two things have to be fixed first

### 1. `Crtime` is stamped with the remote object's mtime

Both creation sites set `Crtime` to the remote mtime, not to the creation time:

- `filer_lazy_remote.go:84-95` — `mtime := time.Unix(remoteEntry.RemoteMtime, 0)`, then `Mtime: mtime, Crtime: mtime`;
- `filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:137-146` — same, defaulting to `time.Now()` only when `RemoteMtime` is absent.

The expiry check is `Crtime + TtlSec < now`. Stamping a TTL as the code stands would expire every object older than the TTL window the instant its entry is created. And in `FindEntry` the expiry branch `return`s at `filer.go:436`, before the lazy-fetch fallback at `:440-446` — so the caller gets `ErrNotFound` for an object that demonstrably exists in the remote. The next request re-creates the entry, which is immediately expired again: objects would alternate 200/404 forever.

So `Crtime` has to mean "when this entry was created", with `Mtime` keeping the remote mtime. That split is arguably just correct on its own merits, independent of TTLs — `Crtime` is currently reporting a fact about the remote object rather than about the entry, and `entryInitialAtime` (`filer.go:395-400`) already prefers `Mtime` where the distinction matters.

### 2. Expiring a directory's last child can delete the remote prefix

This one I did not expect, and it is the reason I am opening an issue rather than a PR.

The entry deletion itself is store-only, as above. But `doListDirectoryEntries` does not stop there — when the expiry pass leaves no valid entries it calls `DeleteEmptyParentDirectories` (`filer.go:502-507`), and that path *does* propagate:

- `IsDirectoryEmpty` (`filer.go:585-592`) calls `f.Store.ListDirectoryPrefixedEntries` directly, bypassing `maybeLazyListFromRemote` — so it sees only the local store and reports the directory empty even though every object is still sitting in the remote;
- it then calls `f.doDeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, dirEntry, false, false, nil)` (`filer.go:573-574`) — `isFromOtherCluster: false`;
- for a directory entry, `maybeDeleteFromRemote` calls `client.RemoveDirectory` (`filer_lazy_remote.go:139-148`);
- `RemoveDirectory` on S3 (`weed/remote_storage/s3/s3_storage_client.go:429`) and GCS (`weed/remote_storage/gcs/gcs_storage_client.go:222`) lists the prefix and **deletes every object under it**.

The only guard is the depth check at `filer.go:550-555`, which protects `/buckets/<bucket>` but nothing below it. So a TTL on lazy entries, added naively, turns "this directory's cached metadata went cold" into "wipe that prefix from the bucket".

It is latent today only because lazy entries carry `TtlSec: 0` and so never reach that code. (The same `isFromOtherCluster: false` call is reachable from the scheduled empty-folder cleaner — `weed/filer/empty_folder_cleanup/empty_folder_cleaner.go:360` — which suggests the interaction between remote mounts and empty-directory cleanup deserves a look regardless of this proposal.)

The fix that fits the existing design is to make `maybeDeleteFromRemote` decline to remove a directory whose emptiness was never confirmed against the remote, or to skip `DeleteEmptyParentDirectories` when the entries were reclaimed by cache expiry rather than deleted by a client. I would rather agree the shape with you than pick one.

## Proposal

Three parts:

1. `Crtime` = creation time at both lazy-creation sites, `Mtime` unchanged. Small and independently defensible.
2. Do not propagate a remote directory removal that originates from cache expiry (see above).
3. Give lazy-created entries a configurable TTL.

For (3), the machinery already exists and I would rather reuse it than add a flag: `FilerConf.PathConf.ttl` (`weed/pb/filer.proto:758`) is already parsed by `needle.ReadTTL` and turned into the entry's `TtlSec` on the upload path (`weed/server/filer_server_handlers_write.go:289-295`). Having the two lazy-creation sites do the same `f.FilerConf.MatchStorageRule(path).GetTtl()` lookup would mean a lazy mount is configured with the command that already exists:

```
fs.configure -locationPrefix=/buckets/mybucket/ -ttl=7d -apply
```

no new proto field, no new flag, and it composes with everything else `filer.conf` already scopes per path. The alternative — a `remote.mount -entryTTL` flag mirroring `-listingCacheTTL` (`weed/shell/command_remote_mount.go:73,93`) — keeps the setting next to the mount it belongs to, at the cost of a second place TTLs come from. I lean towards the `filer.conf` route but have no strong attachment.

## Related

Under a store that expires values natively, there is a second half to this. `redis2`'s directory index leaks a member for every entry whose value key expires, because the listing loop only cleans up on the logical-expiry branch and not on the not-found branch that TTL entries actually take — so TTL-based reclamation frees the values but not the index. Fix in #10735. The two changes compose: TTLs here, and a store that stays clean when they fire.

Background: #8391, #8454, #8522, #8568 are the lazy remote-mount work this builds on. Happy to implement all three parts if the approach sounds right — particularly keen for a steer on (2) before writing anything.

comments.body:
Closing this for now. The section on empty-directory cleanup overstates the risk: `RemoveDirectory` is a no-op on all three remote backends (`gcs_storage_client.go:222`, `s3_storage_client.go:287`, `azure_storage_client.go:380` — all `return nil`), so there is no remote-deletion path there as written. Rather than leave an inaccurate issue standing I'll rework it and re-open with a corrected, simpler proposal.

The `redis2` directory-index fix in #10735 is independent of this and stands on its own.

Correcting my own closing comment above: **it is wrong.** `RemoveDirectory` is not a no-op.

I checked a 4.40 working tree. At 4.40 all three implementations really are `return nil`. At **4.41** they list the prefix and delete every object under it:

- `weed/remote_storage/gcs/gcs_storage_client.go:222-251` — iterates `bucket.Objects(ctx, &storage.Query{Prefix: prefix})` and calls `.Delete()` on each
- `weed/remote_storage/s3/s3_storage_client.go:287+` — `ListObjectsV2Pages` + batched `DeleteObjects`
- `weed/remote_storage/azure/azure_storage_client.go:380+` — `NewListBlobsFlatPager` + per-blob `Delete`

The change is `0d7173a02` "remote storage: actually delete objects when a directory is removed" (#10531), which landed between the two tags. Only the mount root is guarded (`prefix == ""`).

So the concern in the issue body above stands at 4.41, and my retraction of it was mistaken. Apologies for the noise — worth being explicit given the subject matter.

Two things I would flag as still worth a look, independent of the TTL proposal:

**The empty-folder cleaner reaches that code with `isFromOtherCluster = false`.** `deleteFolder` calls `DeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, folder, false, false, false, false, nil, 0)` (`weed/filer/empty_folder_cleanup/empty_folder_cleaner.go:359-360`), so it passes the `!isFromOtherCluster` gate in `filer_delete_entry.go:148-152` and reaches `maybeDeleteFromRemote`. Auto-remove defaults to enabled when the bucket attribute is absent — `autoRemoveEmptyFoldersEnabled` returns `true` for nil attrs, a missing key, or an empty value (`:399-414`) — and the cleaner is fed by `f.triggerLocalEmptyFolderCleanup(...)` at the end of `notifyUpdateEvent` (`weed/filer/filer_notify.go:76`) with no `isFromOtherCluster` gate on that call. So a delete explicitly marked as originating elsewhere can still result in a remote prefix deletion, one level up, via the cleanup it triggers.

**Emptiness is judged against the local store only.** For a lazy remote mount, `IsDirectoryEmpty` consults the store and not the remote, so a directory whose local metadata has been reclaimed reads as empty while its remote objects still exist.

---

Leaving this closed regardless, but for a different reason than the one I gave: the proposal itself cannot be implemented as written. `Filer.UpdateEntry` restores `Crtime` from the stored entry (`weed/filer/filer.go:376-378`) and the gRPC handler zeroes `TtlSec` whenever `Remote != nil` (`weed/server/filer_grpc_server.go:650-653`), so neither field is settable by a client on a remote-mounted entry — which rules out the external-stamping approach I was going to propose alongside it. We are solving our own metadata growth with explicit deletes instead.

If a maintainer thinks the two points above are worth pursuing, I am happy to open a focused issue for them on their own.
